paras: The air-rifle shooting of a Black woman in Savannah took place in the autumn of 1903, when some white boys "seriously" shot an unnamed "colored lady" with an air rifle in the East Broad Street neighborhood of Savannah, Georgia. The only known report, a paragraph in the Black weekly Savannah Tribune, said no attempt was made to apprehend the shooter and cited the case as evidence that white offenders against Black residents went unpunished.

According to the Tribune, the area around East Broad Street had become "a tough one" because of small white boys who were a nuisance to passers-by, "especially colored pedestrians," and at times interfered with them. The paper added that white boys behaved the same way in other parts of the city.

The shooting happened on the Sunday before a small white boy was killed by a trolley car on East Broad Street, in the same neighborhood. Writing on 24 October, the Tribune placed the trolley death "a few Sundays ago," which puts the shooting in late September or early October. The Tribune gave neither the woman's name nor the street, and it described her wound only as serious.
"No attempt was made to apprehend him," the Tribune wrote, and no report of an arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The shooting surfaced only in an editorial paragraph in the Savannah Tribune of 24 October 1903, written in response to the trolley death, which the paper said was the boy's own fault. The Tribune paired the shooting with the earlier fatal cutting of a colored man near the Union station, whose white assailant, it said, had never been brought to justice, and closed with "and thus it is." No report of the shooting was found in the white press, and the Tribune's issue of the previous week did not mention it.

reader.title: Air-rifle shooting of a Black woman in Savannah (1903)
bases: A group of white boys shot a Black woman with an air rifle in a neighborhood where, the Tribune said, white boys interfered with colored pedestrians (A3); no mob in the usual sense is described.
Only one Savannah Tribune editorial paragraph reports the shooting (A3); no white-press report of it was found, and the Tribune's previous issue does not mention it (A2).

accounts.label: Savannah Tribune editorial
accounts.gist: Some white boys seriously shot a colored woman with an air rifle in the East Broad Street neighborhood the Sunday before a white boy's trolley death, and no attempt was made to apprehend the shooter.

framing.detail: The Tribune set the shooting among complaints that white boys on East Broad Street interfered with colored pedestrians and that white men who harmed Black people were not brought to justice, ending "and thus it is."

record_check.dossier: The Sunday before the trolley death; with that death dated Sunday 1903-10-11 by the Morning News, the shooting was on or about 1903-10-04 (inferred).
Shooting with an air rifle only; no beating is reported.
"some white boys"; a group of youths, not a stated mob.
One mention, in the 1903-10-24 Tribune; the 1903-10-17 issue does not mention the shooting.

info: The Sunday before a white boy was killed by a trolley car on East Broad Street, which the Tribune on 1903-10-24 placed "a few Sundays ago"; the Morning News (A1, other episode) dated that death Sunday 1903-10-11, which would put the shooting on or about Sunday 1903-10-04 (inferred).
The same neighborhood as the trolley death on East Broad Street, Savannah

sources.note: Editorial paragraph: white boys on East Broad Street harassed colored pedestrians; the Sunday before the trolley death some white boys shot a colored woman with an air rifle; no attempt to apprehend.
quotes: The Sunday before the boy was killed, in the same neighborhood, some white boys seriously-shot a colored lady with an air rifle.
No attempt was made to apprehend him.
These boys were a nuisance to all who passed that way, especially colored pedestrians; they went at times so far as to interfere with them.

set_aside: Trolley death of ten-year-old Charlie Jackson, white, on East Broad Street on Sunday afternoon (1903-10-11); no mention of the shooting, but it fixes the date of the death the Tribune counts from.
